slides.0.title: Industry and market
slides.0.subtitle: A few large firms lead, and most wine is drunk at home
slides.1.title: Scale: separate two kinds of grape
slides.1.highlights.0.title: A trap in the numbers
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Secondary reports citing the OIV give about 42,000 ha in 2022, but this probably includes table grapes. Variety data from 2002 show only about 10,000 ha for wine and about 39,000 ha for the table
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Output
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Recent output is about 35–40 million bottles a year, with a 1995–2022 average near 350,000 hl. These figures come from press reports, not official statistics
slides.1.highlights.2.title: How to use them
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Remember the scale: behind South Africa in Africa, and far smaller than in the 1950s. If asked for an exact figure, check the source year first
slides.1.content: With Moroccan figures always ask: wine grapes, or all grapes?
slides.2.title: Producers to know
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Les Celliers de Meknès
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The Zniber family business, generally regarded as the largest producer, with Château Roslane in Coteaux de l'Atlas as its flagship
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Castel and Thalvin
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Castel's Boulaouane brand is well known in France. Thalvin runs Domaine des Ouled Thaleb, often described as one of the oldest active wineries
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Val d'Argan
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Near Essaouira on the Atlantic, which lies outside the 14 AOGs: a reminder that good wine need not carry an AOG
slides.2.content: Producer lists change, so remember the types: a domestic giant, French capital and small independents.
slides.3.title: Selling wine in an Islamic country
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Mostly domestic
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Most sources agree that the bulk stays at home and the export share is small, though the exact shares differ
slides.3.highlights.1.title: The 1967 rule
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Article 28 of the 17 July 1967 decree bars licensed sellers from selling alcohol to Moroccan Muslims. Press reports say it remains on the books but is unevenly enforced
slides.3.highlights.2.title: A trace on the label
slides.3.highlights.2.content: The rules also ban any label reference to religious terms, places or buildings, as Level 2 will show
slides.3.content: Legal to produce, restricted to sell and kept low-key: three ideas that explain this market.
